passage:
In the college library, Bidisha's phone buzzed for the fourth time in half an hour. She glanced at it and started typing fast.
"Tanmay?" Ayesha asked.
"He wants a photo of where I'm sitting. He worries." Bidisha snapped the table and sent it. "He's really caring. He even told me which of our group are bad influences."
Ayesha thought of last week: Bidisha leaving the dinner early because Tanmay didn't like the boys there, Bidisha handing over her phone at the canteen so he could scroll her messages.
"Can I ask you something? Not a trick question."
Bidisha nodded.
"With him, or even away from him, do you feel free? Like you could do something he wouldn't pick, and it would be fine?"
Bidisha opened her mouth, then closed it. The phone buzzed again. For a long moment she didn't look at it.

qa.q: What did Tanmay want Bidisha to send?
qa.a: He wanted a photo of where she was sitting.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's long pause before looking at the phone suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ayesha's question unsettled her and she may be realising, perhaps for the first time, that she does not feel free.

qa.q: Why was Ayesha's question a wise way to raise concern?
qa.a: It asked Bidisha to check her own sense of freedom instead of attacking Tanmay, which is less likely to make her defend him.

qa.q: How does Bidisha seem to see Tanmay's checking?
qa.a: She sees it as care and worry, calling him really caring, which shows how control can feel like attention at first.

grounding: A student notices warning signs of control in Tanmay's checking and his say over who Bidisha sees, which she calls caring, and asks her whether she feels free.

passage:
Dear Devika,
I've been thinking about Saturday since I got home. It was lovely to finally meet Kunal when he picked you up. But during our two-hour lunch he texted you five times, asked who each person in your photos was, and said he would prefer you skipped the trek with your college friends. You laughed and said, "He's so protective, na?"
Maybe that's all it is. I don't know him well, and I'm not trying to judge. But when I was your age, someone's protectiveness slowly turned into me asking permission for everything, and I only saw it much later.
So here's the question I wish someone had asked me: do you feel free with him? Free to go on the trek, see your friends, say no without it becoming a big thing?
You don't have to answer me. Just keep asking yourself. And call me any time, about anything.
Love,
Arohi Didi

qa.q: How many times did Kunal text Devika during the lunch?
qa.a: Kunal texted Devika five times during the two-hour lunch.

qa.q: What is Arohi worried about?
qa.a: Arohi worries that Kunal's protectiveness could slowly turn into Devika asking permission for everything, as happened to Arohi.

qa.q: What makes Arohi's letter a helpful approach?
qa.a: It names what Arohi saw without judging, shares a personal experience, offers one question about feeling free, and leaves the door open to call any time.

qa.q: How might Devika feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Devika might feel defensive at first, having called Kunal protective, but the gentle tone and open offer may help Devika quietly check whether that freedom is really there.

grounding: Arohi writes to Devika after noticing Kunal's frequent texts, questions and preferences about the trek, and gently asks whether Devika feels free.

passage:
Pranav, can I tell you something and you don't laugh? Okay. I'm Chetan, and I think I need to say this out loud.
Tanya is great. Really. But in the last two months she's started checking my phone, just "to see who I'm talking to." She said she doesn't like me hanging out with Ravi, so I've kind of stopped. When I went to your birthday, she messaged me every twenty minutes.
Everyone says it's because she cares so much. And it did feel like attention at first. Like someone finally really noticed me.
But last night I was about to text you, and I stopped, because I thought, "What will Tanya say?" That scared me.
My sister asked me something last week: "Do you feel free with her?" I couldn't answer.
So, Pranav. Honestly. From outside. Does this look like caring to you?

qa.q: How often did Tanya message Chetan during the birthday?
qa.a: Every twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he stopped himself from texting Pranav?
qa.a: Chetan felt scared and uneasy, realising every choice was being checked against what Tanya would say.

qa.q: What could Chetan do next?
qa.a: Chetan could keep talking honestly with Pranav and his sister, reconnect with friends like Ravi, and speak to a counsellor about whether he feels free.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Tanya's behaviour from outside?
qa.a: Pranav would likely see the phone checks, friend choices and constant messages as control, not simply caring.

grounding: A young adult describes a partner's phone checking, friend choosing and jealousy framed as care, and uses the question of feeling free as a test.

passage:
I'm Elizabeth, Pallavi's flatmate. I can only tell you what I saw.
At first Pallavi talked about her new boyfriend all the time, happily. He texted her good morning and good night. He wanted to know where she was, "because he worries." She showed me his messages, smiling.
By the second month, she stopped going to our Thursday movie nights. "He doesn't like me being out late." Once I saw him scroll through her phone at our kitchen table while she sat very still.
Then one evening she came into my room and sat on the floor. She said, "Liz, can I ask you something weird? Do you think I'm free? Like, actually free?"
I didn't know what was in her head. I just said, "What do you think?"
She was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "I think I check everything with him first." I made us tea, and we looked up a counselling service together.

qa.q: What did Pallavi stop going to by the second month?
qa.a: Our Thursday movie nights.

qa.q: How did Pallavi seem to feel when she asked if she was free?
qa.a: Pallavi seemed confused and uneasy, starting to sense that the attention had become control.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth do that helped?
qa.a: Elizabeth listened without judging, asked what Pallavi herself thought, and looked up a counselling service with her.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth see the boyfriend's behaviour?
qa.a: Elizabeth notices worrying signs, like the phone scrolling and fewer nights out, but admits not knowing everything Pallavi feels.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young adult slowly recognising a boyfriend's checking and jealousy, described as worry, and asking herself whether she feels free.

passage:
Week one. Rashmi's new boyfriend wanted to see her phone. "I just like knowing everything about you," he said. It felt sweet. Nobody had ever been that interested.
Week three. He said Sabina, her best friend since school, was "a bad influence" and asked Rashmi to see her less. He got quiet and hurt when she went to Sabina's birthday. Rashmi came home early to make him feel better.
Week five. At the college library, Sabina sat down beside her. "You've cancelled on me four times. Are you okay?"
Rashmi opened her mouth to say "he just cares." Then Sabina asked, gently, "Do you feel free with him?"
Rashmi thought of her phone, the early nights, the friend she'd stopped seeing. Her throat went tight.
"No," she said. "I don't think I do."
Sabina held her hand. "Okay. Let's go and see the college counsellor together. Today."

qa.q: How many times had Rashmi cancelled on Sabina?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel when Sabina asked if she felt free?
qa.a: Rashmi felt her throat go tight, suddenly sad and uneasy as she saw how her life had narrowed.

qa.q: What useful test did Sabina offer, and what did they do next?
qa.a: Sabina asked whether Rashmi felt free, and then they went to the college counsellor together that day.

qa.q: How does Sabina see the changes in Rashmi?
qa.a: Sabina is worried, noticing the cancellations and caring enough to ask gently rather than blame.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing over weeks that phone checks, friend choosing and jealousy framed as care leave her not feeling free.

passage: Sit, Pooja. You asked how you know if someone is controlling. Let me tell you about Sunita. We were twenty, in the same college in Nagpur, and she started seeing Mahesh from the hostel. First month, all sweetness. Then he began taking her phone at the canteen and scrolling through it. "I just worry about you," he'd say. He decided she shouldn't come to our study group because "those boys look at you". If she laughed with me, he went cold all evening. Everyone said, he's so caring. I thought so too, at first. What changed my mind was small: Sunita started asking him before ordering her own tea. So I asked her, alone, on the library steps, "Do you feel free with him?" She didn't answer. She just cried. We went to the college counsellor together that week. You know me as Lokesh mama, but back then I was only a worried friend, and that question is still the best one I know.

qa.q: What did Mahesh say when he took Sunita's phone?
qa.a: He said, “I just worry about you.”

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when Sunita started asking permission for her own tea?
qa.a: Lokesh felt worried and uneasy, because the small sign showed the so-called caring was taking away Sunita's freedom.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made a difference?
qa.a: Asking Sunita alone whether she felt free with Mahesh, then going with her to the college counsellor, gave her a safe way to face what was happening.

qa.q: How might Sunita have experienced Mahesh's attention at the start?
qa.a: At first it probably felt like love and care, which is why the control was hard to see until Lokesh's question made her cry.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a friend's partner checking her phone, choosing her friends and turning jealous, all described as care, and asking whether she feels free.
